div.p: The skull base is an intricate interface between the cranium and the face. Both intracranial and extracranial pathologies can occur at this location. Although the tumor origin is clear in most cases, certain extracranial tumors may mimic primary intracranial pathologies. A 48-year-old woman with a history of resection of a right tentorial meningioma 17 years earlier presented with worsening right facial palsy. No obvious enlargement of the parotid gland was noted. Imaging revealed a residual tentorial meningioma and a homogenously enhancing mass extending alongside the right facial nerve. The patient underwent several biopsies, and the diagnosis of adenoid cystic carcinoma arising from the parotid gland was made. She subsequently underwent carbon-ion radiation therapy and remained stable for 28 months after surgery. The representative case reiterates the importance of evaluating both intracranial and extracranial pathologies when a clinician encounters skull base tumors, especially those with perineural spreading. The tendency of meningiomas to involve the trigeminal nerve while sparing the facial nerve may provide a clue for the differential diagnosis.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The skull base represents the inferior aspect of the neurocranium and serves as an interface between the extracranial and intracranial compartments. 1,2) Hence, not only do primarily intracranial pathologies involve the skull base, but extracranial pathologies may also invade and traverse the skull base, spreading intracranially. 2) Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is a rare malignant tumor of extracranial origin that primarily involves the salivary glands. 3) Biphasic glandular structures composed of abluminal myoepithelial cells and luminal ductal cells are characteristic of ACC. [3][4][5] ACC demonstrates indolent, locally invasive growth with a high propensity for locoregional recurrence and metastasis. [6][7][8] Although local temporal bone invasion by ACC has been described repeatedly, [9][10][11] cases of ACC presenting as a solid intracranial mass are rarely reported, as far as our search revealed. We encountered a case of an occult parotid gland tumor without apparent enlargement, traveling along the facial nerve and presenting as a skull base tumor. div.head: Case Report
div.p: A 48-year-old woman presented to our department with progressive right facial palsy over several months. Her past medical history included resection of a right tentorial meningioma 17 years earlier (Fig. 1A), with a histopathological diagnosis of transitional meningioma, World Health Organization grade I. A small amount of tumor remained (Fig. 1B), and she developed mild facial palsy following surgery. She did not receive any adjuvant radiation therapy after the initial procedure. At presentation, neurological examination revealed severe dysfunction of the right facial nerve. Her face appeared asymmetric at rest. She could not fully close her right eye and could only slightly move her mouth. No other cranial nerve abnormalities were detected. Her gait was stable, and ataxia was not evident. Muscle strength and tone of the limbs were normal bilaterally. The sensory system was intact. Swelling of the parotid gland was not initially apparent, and no tenderness was present.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a homogenously enhancing residual lesion at the right tentorial incisura (Fig. 1C) and a homogenously enhancing mass involving the arcuate eminence (Fig. 1D), spreading along the facial nerve (Fig. 1E), and extending to the parotid gland (Fig. 1 F). The parotid gland exhibited no apparent enlargement on imaging compared to the contralateral side, although abnormal contrast enhancement was present (Fig. 2A). No other systemic lesions were detected on computed tomography and positron-emission tomography (Fig. 2B), reducing the likelihood of metastasis. A 3-dimensional computer graphic was created for preoperative simulation. The anatomical relationship among the mass, residual meningioma, trigeminal, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves, and parotid gland was depicted (Fig. 2C-E). Differential diagnoses included recurrence and perineural spread of a tentorial meningioma, facial nerve schwannoma, malignant lymphoma, and perineural spread of a parotid gland tumor. Considering the history of resection of the tentorial meningioma several years earlier, recurrence of the meningioma was initially the top differential diagnosis.

To obtain a pathological diagnosis, a surgical biopsy was proposed. The patient and her family consented to the treatment. Under general anesthesia, the lesion was accessed via temporal craniotomy. A biopsy of the tumor was performed, and the specimen was sent to the pathology department. The patient recovered quickly from anesthesia without any complications. Postoperative imaging revealed residual tumor without obvious complications (Fig. 3A). She experienced no neurological deterioration during the perioperative course. Histopathological evaluation revealed a mixture of cribriform and tubular patterns (Fig. 3B). The histopathological diagnosis of ACC was made.

She was referred to an otolaryngologist and underwent a biopsy of the parotid gland tumor. Considering the histopathological diagnosis of the intracranial pathology and its continuity with the parotid gland, she was diagnosed with extension of the parotid gland ACC. She underwent further treatment with carbon-ion radiation therapy (64 Gy/16 fractions) due to the inoperable stage of the tumor. She has been monitored with regular imaging follow-ups (Fig. 3C). She is still alive and free from recurrence 28 months after the histopathological diagnosis.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: We present a case of an occult parotid gland tumor infiltrating along the facial nerve and appearing as a skull base tumor. Because the patient had previously undergone resection of a tentorial meningioma several years earlier and the swelling of the parotid gland was subtle, the possibility of an extracranial origin was initially overlooked. We highlight the importance of considering an extracranial origin, particularly in cases with ascending perineural spread, as a differential diagnosis of skull base tumors. Additionally, we aim to elucidate the characteristics of ascending perineural spread of extracranial tumors and the perineural spread of meningiomas by appraising the literature.

Perineural spread is one of the tumor extension patterns, referring to contiguous tumor growth along a nerve. 12,13) The nerve provides a conduit for the tumor to traverse both in anterograde and retrograde fashion. 14,15) The tumor spreads along the nerve and reaches a site separate from the primary lesion. 16) This phenomenon occurs due to complex crosstalk between tumor cells, nerves, and the microenvironment. 17) Neurotropic factors, matrix metalloproteinases, cell adhesion molecules, and tumor growth factors are involved in the process occurring at the perineural niche. 18) Several malignancies, including those of the pancreas, prostate, colorectum, and head and neck, are known for their predilection for perineural spread. 17) In the head and neck region, nasopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, lymphoma, desmoplastic melanoma, and ACC of the salivary glands are particularly known for their tendency towards perineural spread. 6,14) These tumors may extend along the cranial nerve and infiltrate the skull base.

Due to its anatomical proximity and neurotropic nature, ACC of the parotid gland commonly involves the facial nerve and may cause peripheral facial palsy. 14, [19][20][21] Facial nerve involvement is recognized as a sign of disease progression and is one of the criteria used to grade tumor extent. 19) Tumors may extend centripetally toward the brain, traverse the skull base foramina, and emerge at deeper intracranial destinations. 20) In our case, the tumor even reached the geniculate ganglion. With careful evaluation, nerve enlargement and erosion of the skull base foramina may be observed. 21) ACC is notorious for its neurotropic nature and may spread not only along the facial nerve but also the trigeminal, 17) vagus, 22) or hypoglossal nerves. 23) Clinicians should consider occult ACC in the differential diagnosis when patients present with neuropathic pain or cranial nerve paralysis without an obvious lesion.

Because our representative patient had undergone resection of a meningioma adjacent to the intracranial facial nerve, recurrence of the meningioma was initially regarded as the most likely diagnosis. Meningioma is an extra-axial, dural-based tumor 24,25) and is recognized as a tumor that rarely causes perineural spread. 6,14) While ACC directly invades the perineurium and traverses along the nerve, meningioma does not invade the perineurium but instead uses the nerve as a scaffold and exit path. 6,21) Furthermore, it is noteworthy that all previously reported cases of meningioma with perineural spread solely involved the trigeminal nerve. The trigeminal nerve becomes uncovered by meningeal layers at the cisternal portion shortly after exiting the brainstem, leaving the perineurium exposed and thereby facilitating tumor cell entry and spread. By contrast, the facial nerve remains ensheathed for most of its intracranial and intratemporal course within the internal auditory canal and the facial canal, structures encased by dura and bone that may function as physical barriers against direct perineural invasion. 6,14,17) Since our case showed perineural spread along the facial nerve, this finding may have been key in differentiating the possibility of perineural spreading of meningioma.

Although the parotid gland represented the primary site of disease, fine-needle aspiration biopsy failed to yield malignant findings. This discrepancy highlights the wellrecognized limitations of cytological assessment in salivary gland tumors. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy is inherently subject to the risk of misclassification, particularly in the context of myoepithelial-rich or lymphoid-rich lesions, where overlapping cytomorphological features can obscure malignant components. 26) Furthermore, tumor heterogeneity and sampling error may contribute to false-negative results. These considerations underscore the importance of interpreting biopsy results with caution.

Perineural spread implies a grave prognosis, with a proclivity for recurrence and metastasis. 21) Perineural spread occurs through both centripetal and centrifugal growth, and the skull base offers many avenues through which cranial nerves can be invaded. When clinicians encounter perineural spread of a tumor of unknown origin, both intracranial and extracranial pathologies should be thoroughly evaluated, and the neurotropic nature of ACC should be kept in mind. Furthermore, the poor prognosis associated with perineural spread should be recognized, and a precise evaluation of the extent of tumor infiltration is mandatory.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Ascending perineural spread of ACC of the parotid gland mimicked a recurrence of skull base meningioma. Extracranial tumors should be considered in the differential diagnosis of skull base tumors, especially when perineural spread is observed. The inclination of meningioma to involve the trigeminal nerve while sparing the facial nerve might serve as a clue for diagnosis.
